fossa.outlook: Researchers estimate there may be only a few thousand adult fossas left. Because fossas need such large territories, even big protected areas may hold only a few dozen.

kea.outlook: Volunteers now build predator traps around kea nesting areas and fit nests with cameras, and early results show far more chicks surviving where stoats are controlled.

secretarybird.outlook: Collisions with fences and power lines kill many young birds. In South Africa, researchers are tracking secretarybirds with GPS tags to learn where they travel and what dangers they meet.

superb-lyrebird.outlook: Encouragingly, surveys after the 2019–2020 fires found lyrebirds surviving in unburnt gullies and returning to recovering forest, and their digging helps the burnt forest floor recover by mixing ash and leaf litter into the soil.

gharial.outlook: In recent years, hatchlings have been found again in some rivers where gharials had disappeared, a sign that release programmes can work when rivers are protected, and local 'gharial guardians' now watch over nesting beaches.

thorny-devil.family: Hatchlings are only about 6 centimetres long and weigh under 2 grams, yet they already have their full coat of spikes. They grow slowly and take three to five years to reach adult size, eating ants from their very first days above ground.

blandings-turtle.family: Hatchlings are about the size of a large coin, with dark shells and long tails. In their first years they hide among dense plants in shallow water, where they are hunted by herons, fish, frogs and snapping turtles. Very few eggs ever produce an adult turtle, which is why each adult female matters so much.

glass-frog.family: Male reticulated glass frogs often guard eggs from several females at once and may sit on or beside them for weeks, even through the day. Researchers have found that eggs left without a guarding father are far more likely to dry out or be eaten by wasps and fly larvae, so this care makes a real difference.

hellbender.outlook: Volunteers in several states now help scientists survey streams, and in some places specially designed concrete 'nest boxes' are placed in rivers to give hellbenders safe places to breed.

ocean-sunfish.outlook: Researchers now tag sunfish with satellite tags to track their migrations and learn which fishing areas are most dangerous for them, information that can help fisheries reduce bycatch.

leafy-seadragon.family: Each newborn seadragon is about 2 centimetres long and immediately begins hunting tiny plankton. Only a small fraction survive their first weeks, when fish and other predators eat many of them. Those that survive grow quickly and can reach their adult size within about a year.

coelacanth.outlook: In the Comoros, protected marine areas and fishing education programmes have helped reduce accidental catches, and divers and submersibles now monitor the caves where coelacanths shelter.

greenland-shark.outlook: Scientists tag Greenland sharks with satellite trackers to learn where they travel. Some have been followed for long journeys between Greenland and Canada. Better data could help fisheries avoid accidentally catching these ancient animals.

blue-dragon.family: A single blue dragon can lay many strings of eggs during its life, and because each animal can lay eggs, populations can grow quickly when food is plentiful. Scientists still know little about how long blue dragons live or how they find mates in the vast open ocean, but the blue fleets that gather in certain winds may help bring them together.

vampire-squid.outlook: Researchers are studying how low-oxygen zones in the ocean are changing as the climate warms. Because the vampire squid is adapted to these zones, it could help scientists understand how deep-sea life copes with changes in oxygen.

coconut-crab.outlook: On some islands, such as parts of Vanuatu and the Cook Islands, communities have set aside areas where coconut crabs cannot be harvested, and these areas help larger crabs survive and breed.

atlas-moth.family: Atlas moth caterpillars molt several times as they grow and become covered in a white, waxy powder that may help protect them from predators and moisture. They eat a wide range of plants, which helps the species survive in gardens and farmland. The caterpillar's cocoon is tough and papery, wrapped in leaves, and the adult escapes through a one-way opening at one end. Females often stay near the cocoon they emerged from, waiting for males to find them.

orchid-mantis.family: Female orchid mantises are much larger than males and live longer. Males reach adulthood sooner and must find a female quickly, guided partly by scent. Because females sometimes eat males, males approach cautiously. Mantis nymphs are hunters from the moment they hatch, eating tiny flies and other insects. Young orchid mantises are highly cannibalistic, so siblings soon spread out across the forest, each looking for a good place to ambush its prey.

green-darner.family: Green darner nymphs breathe through gills inside their rear ends, drawing water in and out. By forcing the water out quickly, they can shoot forward like a jet to escape predators. Nymphs can take a few months to almost a year to develop, depending on temperature. When they are ready, they climb out of the water, often at night, and split their skin. The new adult pumps fluid into its wings to expand them and takes several hours before it can fly.

hercules-beetle.family: Hercules beetle larvae go through three stages, called instars, growing larger each time they molt. In the final stage, a larva can be longer than an adult's body and much heavier. When it is ready to pupate, it builds a chamber in the soil or wood, using its own droppings and saliva to strengthen the walls. Males need a larger chamber than females to make space for their growing horns. They emerge as adults after about two months.
